deletion_policy.description:
Whether Terraform will be prevented from destroying the instance. Defaults to "DELETE".
When a 'terraform destroy' or 'terraform apply' would delete the instance,
the command will fail if this field is set to "PREVENT" in Terraform state.
When set to "ABANDON", the command will remove the resource from Terraform
management without updating or deleting the resource in the API.
When set to "DELETE", deleting the resource is allowed.
deletion_policy.rationale: If deletion_policy is left at the default value of DELETE, the autoscaler can be destroyed accidentally via terraform destroy or apply, removing active scaling management and potentially causing a service outage. Policy should require deletion_policy to be set to PREVENT.

description.description: An optional description of this resource.
description.rationale: description is a free-text label field with no functional effect on resource behaviour, so it carries no security impact.

name.description:
Name of the resource. The name must be 1-63 characters long and match
the regular expression '[a-z]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?' which means the
first character must be a lowercase letter, and all following
characters must be a dash, lowercase letter, or digit, except the last
character, which cannot be a dash.
name.rationale: name is a required identifier constrained by GCP's own naming regex, it does not control any behaviour, permissions, or scaling logic, so no direct security impact is identified.

project.description: The ID of the project in which the resource belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
project.rationale: If project is left unset, the resource defaults to the provider's project context, which risks the autoscaler being deployed into the wrong project (for e.g. a shared or less-restricted enviroment) without explicit confirmation. Policy should require project to be explicitly set to avoid accidental cross-project deployment.

region.description: URL of the region where the instance group resides.
region.rationale: Determines the region/zone where the resource is created. Policy should restrict it to an approved-region whitelist for data residency; the allowed set is parameterised (a hardcoded example whitelist is acceptable).

target.description: URL of the managed instance group that this autoscaler will scale.
target.rationale: If target points to an unintended or incorrectly-scoped managed instance group, the autoscaler could apply scaling actions to the wrong workload, causing unintended capacity changes to an unrelated service, an integrity/availability risk under the CIA triad. Policy should verify target references a valid, intended instance group.

autoscaling_policy.description:
The configuration parameters for the autoscaling algorithm. You can
define one or more of the policies for an autoscaler: cpuUtilization,
customMetricUtilizations, and loadBalancingUtilization.

If none of these are specified, the default will be to autoscale based
on cpuUtilization to 0.6 or 60%.

autoscaling_policy.cooldown_period.description:
The number of seconds that the autoscaler should wait before it
starts collecting information from a new instance. This prevents
the autoscaler from collecting information when the instance is
initializing, during which the collected usage would not be
reliable. The default time autoscaler waits is 60 seconds.

Virtual machine initialization times might vary because of
numerous factors. We recommend that you test how long an
instance may take to initialize. To do this, create an instance
and time the startup process.
autoscaling_policy.cooldown_period.rationale: If cooldown_period is set too short, the autoscaler collects metrics from instances still initializing, causing it to make scaling decisions based on unreliable data. Policy should require a sensible minimum cooldown_period matching realistic instance startup time.

autoscaling_policy.max_replicas.description:
The maximum number of instances that the autoscaler can scale up
to. This is required when creating or updating an autoscaler. The
maximum number of replicas should not be lower than minimal number
of replicas.
autoscaling_policy.max_replicas.rationale: If max_replicas is not set to a sensible limit, the autoscaler can keep adding servers indefinitely during a traffic spike, leading to a massive, unexpected cloud bill - an attack known as Denial of Wallet. Policy should require max_replicas to be set to a reasonable, capped value.

autoscaling_policy.min_replicas.description:
The minimum number of replicas that the autoscaler can scale down
to. This cannot be less than 0. If not provided, autoscaler will
choose a default value depending on maximum number of instances
allowed.
autoscaling_policy.min_replicas.rationale: If min_replicas is set to 0, the autoscaler can scale down to zero running servers, causing a denial-of-service outcome (an availability failure under the CIA triad) even without any attacker involved. policy should require min_replicas to be atleast 1.

autoscaling_policy.mode.description: Defines operating mode for this policy.
autoscaling_policy.mode.rationale: If mode is set to OFF, the autoscaler stops responding to load entirely, leaving the instance group fixed in size and unable to scale out during a traffic spike, an availability failure under the CIA triad. Policy should require mode to be set to ON (or ONLY_UP at minimum) so the autoscaler remains active

autoscaling_policy.stabilization_period.description:
The number of seconds that the autoscaler waits for load stabilization
before making scale-in decisions.

This might appear as a delay in scaling in but it is an important mechanism
for your application to not have fluctuating size due to short term load
fluctuations.
autoscaling_policy.stabilization_period.rationale: If stabilization_period is set too low, the autoscaler can scale in prematurely based on short-term dips in load, then be unable to respond fast enough to a subsequent spike, risking an availability failure under the CIA triad. Policy should require a sensible minimum stabilization_period.

autoscaling_policy.cpu_utilization.description:
Defines the CPU utilization policy that allows the autoscaler to
scale based on the average CPU utilization of a managed instance
group.

autoscaling_policy.cpu_utilization.predi.description:
Indicates whether predictive autoscaling based on CPU metric is enabled. Valid values are:

- NONE (default). No predictive method is used. The autoscaler scales the group to meet current demand based on real-time metrics.

- OPTIMIZE_AVAILABILITY. Predictive autoscaling improves availability by monitoring daily and weekly load patterns and scaling out ahead of anticipated demand.
autoscaling_policy.cpu_utilization.predi.rationale: predictive_method controls whether scaling uses historical load patterns to anticipate demand versus reacting only to real-time metrics. It's a performance/smoothness optimisation rather than a control whose misconfiguaration creates a secuirty or availability gap, so no security impact is assigned.

autoscaling_policy.cpu_utilization.targe.description:
The target CPU utilization that the autoscaler should maintain.
Must be a float value in the range (0, 1]. If not specified, the
default is 0.6.

If the CPU level is below the target utilization, the autoscaler
scales down the number of instances until it reaches the minimum
number of instances you specified or until the average CPU of
your instances reaches the target utilization.

If the average CPU is above the target utilization, the autoscaler
scales up until it reaches the maximum number of instances you
specified or until the average utilization reaches the target
utilization.
autoscaling_policy.cpu_utilization.targe.rationale: Setting cpu_utilization.target too close to 1.0 leaves little headroom for the autoscaler to react before instances become overloaded, risking service degradation or outage during a sudden traffic burst. Policy should require target to stay within a sensible range that preserves scaling headroom

autoscaling_policy.load_balancing_utiliz.description: Configuration parameters of autoscaling based on a load balancer.

Fraction of backend capacity utilization (set in HTTP(s) load
balancing configuration) that autoscaler should maintain. Must
be a positive float value. If not defined, the default is 0.8.
autoscaling_policy.load_balancing_utiliz.rationale: If load_balancing_utilization.target is set too close to 1.0, backend capacity leaves little headroom to absorb a sudden traffic surge, risking overloaded backends. Policy should require target to stay within a sensible range that preserves headroom.

autoscaling_policy.metric.description: Configuration parameters of autoscaling based on a custom metric.

autoscaling_policy.metric.filter.description:
A filter string to be used as the filter string for
a Stackdriver Monitoring TimeSeries.list API call.
This filter is used to select a specific TimeSeries for
the purpose of autoscaling and to determine whether the metric
is exporting per-instance or per-group data.

You can only use the AND operator for joining selectors.
You can only use direct equality comparison operator (=) without
any functions for each selector.
You can specify the metric in both the filter string and in the
metric field. However, if specified in both places, the metric must
be identical.

The monitored resource type determines what kind of values are
expected for the metric. If it is a gce_instance, the autoscaler
expects the metric to include a separate TimeSeries for each
instance in a group. In such a case, you cannot filter on resource
labels.

If the resource type is any other value, the autoscaler expects
this metric to contain values that apply to the entire autoscaled
instance group and resource label filtering can be performed to
point autoscaler at the correct TimeSeries to scale upon.
This is called a per-group metric for the purpose of autoscaling.

If not specified, the type defaults to gce_instance.

You should provide a filter that is selective enough to pick just
one TimeSeries for the autoscaled group or for each of the instances
(if you are using gce_instance resource type). If multiple
TimeSeries are returned upon the query execution, the autoscaler
will sum their respective values to obtain its scaling value.
autoscaling_policy.metric.filter.rationale: If metric.filter is too broad or misconfigured, the autoscaler may aggregate or select the wrong TimeSeries data, leading to inaccurate scaling decisions and potential availability issues. Policy should require metric.filter to be scoped precisely to the intended metric source.

autoscaling_policy.metric.name.description:
The identifier (type) of the Stackdriver Monitoring metric.
The metric cannot have negative values.

The metric must have a value type of INT64 or DOUBLE.
autoscaling_policy.metric.name.rationale: If metric_name reference an unreliable, unmonitored, or incorrect metric, the autoscaler will make scaling decisions based on faulty signals, potentially failing to scale out under real load, an availability risk under the CIA triad. Policy should require metric.name to reference a validated, actively-monitored metric.

autoscaling_policy.metric.single_instanc.description:
If scaling is based on a per-group metric value that represents the
total amount of work to be done or resource usage, set this value to
an amount assigned for a single instance of the scaled group.
The autoscaler will keep the number of instances proportional to the
value of this metric, the metric itself should not change value due
to group resizing.

For example, a good metric to use with the target is
'pubsub.googleapis.com/subscription/num_undelivered_messages'
or a custom metric exporting the total number of requests coming to
your instances.

A bad example would be a metric exporting an average or median
latency, since this value can't include a chunk assignable to a
single instance, it could be better used with utilization_target
instead.
autoscaling_policy.metric.single_instanc.rationale: If single_instance assignment is set too high, the autoscaler under-provisions instances relative to actual per-instance workload capacity, risking overloaded instances and an availability failure under the CIA triad. Policy should require a realistic single_instance_assignment value.

autoscaling_policy.metric.target.description:
The target value of the metric that autoscaler should
maintain. This must be a positive value. A utilization
metric scales number of virtual machines handling requests
to increase or decrease proportionally to the metric.

For example, a good metric to use as a utilizationTarget is
www.googleapis.com/compute/instance/network/received_bytes_count.
The autoscaler will work to keep this value constant for each
of the instances.
autoscaling_policy.metric.target.rationale: If metric.target is set too high, the autoscaler waits too long to scale out, risking service degradation under load. Policy should require metric.target to be set to a value that leaves adequate scaling headroom.

autoscaling_policy.metric.type.description:
Defines how target utilization value is expressed for a
Stackdriver Monitoring metric. Possible values: ["GAUGE", "DELTA_PER_SECOND", "DELTA_PER_MINUTE"]
autoscaling_policy.metric.type.rationale: type only defines how the metric's numeric value is interpreted (gauge vs delta); it does not itself introduce a misconfiguration risk independent of the metric.target and metric.filer settings already covered.

autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.description:
Defines scale in controls to reduce the risk of response latency
and outages due to abrupt scale-in events

autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.time.description:
How long back autoscaling should look when computing recommendations
to include directives regarding slower scale down, as described above.
autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.time.rationale: If time_window_sec is set too low, the autoscaler bases scale-in decisions on a very narrow, recent snapshot of load, making it prone to misreading a brief lull as sustained low demand and scaling in prematurely, an availability risk under the CIA triad. policy should require a sensible minimum time_window_sec to smooth out scale-in decisions.

autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.max_.description:
Specifies a fixed number of VM instances. This must be a positive
integer.
autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.max_.rationale: If max_scaled_in_replicas.fixed is left unset, the autoscaler can remove a large number of instances in a single scale-in event, riskinga sudden drop in serving capacity and an availability failure under the CIA triad if load returns quickly. Policy should require a sensible fixed cap on scale-in size.

autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.max_.description:
Specifies a percentage of instances between 0 to 100%, inclusive.
For example, specify 80 for 80%.
autoscaling_policy.scale_in_control.max_.rationale: If max_scaled_in_replicas.percent is left unbounded (upto 100%), the autoscaler could remove the entire managed instance group in a single scale-in event, causing a self-inflicted availability outage under the CIA triad. Policy should require a sensible cap on the scale-in percentage.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.description: Scaling schedules defined for an autoscaler. Multiple schedules can be set on an autoscaler and they can overlap.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.des.description: A description of a scaling schedule.
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.des.rationale: description is a free-text label field with no functional effect on resource behaviour, so it carries no security impact.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.dis.description: A boolean value that specifies if a scaling schedule can influence autoscaler recommendations. If set to true, then a scaling schedule has no effect.
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.dis.rationale: If disabled is set to true unintentionally, the scaling schedule has no effect and the group will not scale as expected during the intended demand window. Policy should require disabled to be explicitly reviewed and set to false for active schedules.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.dur.description: The duration of time intervals (in seconds) for which this scaling schedule will be running. The minimum allowed value is 300.
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.dur.rationale: If duration_sec is set too short, the scaling schedule may end before the actual demand window passed, casuing the group to scale back down prematurely. Policy should require duration_sec to adequately cover the intended demand window.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.min.description: Minimum number of VM instances that autoscaler will recommend in time intervals starting according to schedule.
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.min.rationale: If min_required_replicas is set to 0 or too low for a scheduled high-demand window, the group may be under-provisioned exactly when load is expected to be highest, an availability risk under the CIA triad. Policy should require min_required_replicas to be set to a sensible non-zero value.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.nam.rationale: name is an identifier label for the schedule with no functional effect on scaling behaviour, so it carries no security impact.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.sch.description: The start timestamps of time intervals when this scaling schedule should provide a scaling signal. This field uses the extended cron format (with an optional year field).
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.sch.rationale: If schedule is misconfigured with an incorrect cron expression, the scaling schedule may fail to trigger at the intended time, leaving the group under-provisioned during an expected demand window. Policy should require schedule to be validated against expected demand patterns.

autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.tim.description: The time zone to be used when interpreting the schedule. The value of this field must be a time zone name from the tz database: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tz_database.
autoscaling_policy.scaling_schedules.tim.rationale: If time_zone is left unset or incorrect, the scaling schedule may trigger at the wrong actual time relative to real demand patterns, causing the group to scale out too late, an availability risk under the CIA triad. Policy should require time_zone to be explicitly and correctly set.
